svg.text: Species do not run out. They get logarithmically more expensive.

predicted minus actual, as a share of actual
Each mark is one class, spread vertically only so they can be told apart.
The saturating fit lands entirely left of zero — every class has already
passed the ceiling a century of its own data implied, so that model cannot
be used to argue a group is nearly described. A power law overshoots almost
as consistently. The log-linear fit straddles zero, which is what makes the
right-hand panel legible at all; its mean absolute error is still 15%, so
read the ranking, not the digits.
what the next hundred species cost
records that must be added to the class, from the log-linear fit
species the class already has in OBIS
Sponges and sea snails are the cheapest in the register and seabirds the
dearest by a factor of 765. That is not a size effect: sponges hold 6,627
species against the seabirds' 1,232, so the group with five times the
species is three orders of magnitude cheaper to extend. OBIS takes in
roughly 7.5M records a year across everything, which makes 100 more sponge
species about four days of global intake and 100 more seabird species about
eight and a half years of it.
OBIS v3 checklist with an enddate cut-off and statistics/years, fetched 2026-09-18. The horizontal axis of the accumulation curve is the date ON the
record, never the date it became known: a specimen collected in 1911 may have been keyed in in 2019, so this is what OBIS now holds dated on or before
a year, not what was known in that year. A fitted ceiling is a ceiling on this register, bounded by what gets observed, digitised and submitted — a
group nobody surveys has a low ceiling for that reason and not a biological one.
